analysis.one_liner: Adds dental and oral health coverage — cleanings, fillings, root canals, dentures — to Medicare.
analysis.headline: The Medicare Dental Benefit Act never got a hearing or a vote in either committee it was sent to, and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025, with only 2 House sponsors behind it.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have written dental care into Medicare for the first time. It would cover routine cleanings, exams, and x-rays; basic work like fillings and extractions; major work like root canals, crowns, and dentures; and emergency dental care — all of which Medicare excludes today. Medicare's payment share would start at 0% and climb 10 points a year to 80%, though low-income beneficiaries would get the full 80% immediately. The bill was referred to two House committees and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 65 million people on Medicare, who currently pay out of pocket for nearly all dental care or go without it. Older adults would get coverage for cleanings, fillings, root canals, crowns, dentures, and emergency dental treatment. Low-income beneficiaries would see Medicare pick up 80% of the cost right away, and states would be reimbursed 100% by the federal government for the Medicare cost-sharing they cover for dental services for qualified beneficiaries.

how_it_helps.text: Medicare today expressly excludes dental services; the bill strikes that exclusion and makes dental and oral health services a covered benefit, including preventive care, basic services, and major services like root canals, crowns, and dentures.
Emergency dental care would be covered, addressing situations where untreated oral infections send seniors to emergency rooms.
Low-income beneficiaries ('subsidy eligible individuals') would get Medicare paying 80% of dental costs from the first year, rather than waiting through the phase-in.
Dental prostheses — full and partial dentures — would be covered, with a limit of one set every five years and Medicare covering 80% after the phase-in.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government and taxpayers, through higher Medicare spending; the bill includes no dedicated financing or offset. Beneficiaries would also pay meaningful cost-sharing in the early years, because Medicare's payment share starts at 0% and only reaches 80% in the eighth year after the payment system takes effect. Dentists would face Medicare payment rates and frequency limits (two cleanings and two exams per year; dentures once every five years).

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no funding mechanism or revenue offset, so the full cost of a new open-ended Medicare benefit would be added to the federal deficit.

The phase-in is slow: Medicare pays 0% of dental costs in the first year and only ramps up 10 percentage points a year to 80%, so beneficiaries would still face substantial out-of-pocket costs for years after enactment.

Coverage is limited: two cleanings and two exams per 12 months, dentures only once every five years, and the Health and Human Services Secretary could impose additional limits or prior-authorization requirements.
Dentist participation is not guaranteed — Medicare rates are often lower than private dental fees, which could limit how many practices actually accept Medicare patients.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and large for a population that today pays dental bills entirely out of pocket or skips care, and poor oral health is linked to broader medical problems. But the design softens the benefit: a multi-year phase-in with rising cost-sharing delays relief, and the absence of any funding mechanism makes the bill an aspiration rather than finished legislation. The generous immediate coverage for low-income beneficiaries is the strongest feature.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in two House committees for the rest of the Congress — it was referred to subcommittee but never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Nanette Barragan introduced the Medicare Dental Benefit Act on June 15, 2023, joined by Representative Robin Kelly of Illinois.
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, the two panels with jurisdiction over Medicare.
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, where it remained; no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded in its action history.
The bill attracted only one cosponsor in a 435-member House and died at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025, without ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare beneficiaries gained nothing and keep paying full price for dental care out of pocket. The status quo also serves Medicare Advantage plans and standalone dental insurers, who continue selling dental coverage as an add-on product rather than seeing it folded into basic Medicare.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Dental insurers and MA plans keep the status quo

for.name: Rep. Nanette Barragan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to add a dental benefit to Medicare.

for.name: Rep. Robin Kelly
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no other member joined.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health Subcommittee and never held a hearing or markup; it died there.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral for its share of the bill and took no further action recorded.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so the partisan split never got tested; both sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsor signed on, but with only two sponsors the record shows inattention rather than organized opposition.

industries.note: A universal Medicare dental benefit would create a huge new paying patient population for dental practices. Their interest in the bill runs alongside beneficiaries', though Medicare payment limits and rates temper the gain.

Millions of people buy separate dental policies or dental discount plans because Medicare excludes dental care; a comprehensive Medicare dental benefit would erode that market. Their interest in keeping dental out of Medicare runs against beneficiaries who need coverage.

MA plans use limited dental benefits as a selling point to attract enrollees; a universal Medicare dental benefit would remove that marketing edge, though MA plans would still administer care under Medicare rules.
